summary.text: A nonzero determinant forces at least one matrix entry to be nonzero, and that entry supplies two primes whose sum is \((n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n\). For \(k\ge 60\), taking the odd integer \(n=2k+1>120\) therefore gives a prime decomposition of \(4k+2\), while the cases \(1\le k<60\) are handled by explicit prime pairs.

full_proof.text:
Let \(A(n)\) denote the sequence term defined as follows. For \(n\ge 0\), form the \(n\times n\) integer matrix \(M_n\), whose rows and columns are indexed by \(i,j\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\), and put
\[
 (M_n)_{ij}=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Here the displayed differences agree with natural-number subtraction: because \(i,j<n\), we have \(j<n\le n+i\) and \(i<n\le n+j\), so neither subtraction is truncated. Then
\[
 A(n)=\det(M_n).
\]

We first establish the determinant consequence on which the argument rests.

**Lemma.** If \(n>0\) and \(A(n)\ne 0\), then there are primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
p+q=2n.
\]

Indeed, for any two row and column indices \(i,j<n\), define
\[
p_{ij}=n+i-j,\qquad q_{ij}=n+j-i.
\]
As noted above, these are ordinary nonnegative integer differences, and cancellation gives
\[
p_{ij}+q_{ij}=(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n. \tag{1}
\]
Suppose, contrary to the conclusion of the lemma, that no two primes have sum \(2n\). If an entry \((M_n)_{ij}\) were \(1\), then by definition both \(p_{ij}\) and \(q_{ij}\) would be prime; equation (1) would then exhibit two primes whose sum is \(2n\), a contradiction. Thus every entry of \(M_n\) is zero, so \(M_n\) is the zero matrix. Since \(n>0\), the determinant of this zero \(n\times n\) matrix is zero (equivalently, every product in the Leibniz determinant expansion contains a zero factor). This contradicts \(A(n)=\det(M_n)\ne0\). The lemma follows.

Now assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement:
\[
\text{for every odd integer }n>120,\qquad A(n)\ne0. \tag{2}
\]
We prove that every integer \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is a sum of two primes.

First consider the finite range \(1\le k<60\). The following table gives, for each such \(k\), primes \(p,q\) satisfying \(p+q=4k+2\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|r@{\qquad}c|r@{\qquad}c|r}
k&(p,q)&k&(p,q)&k&(p,q)\\ \hline
1&(3,3)&21&(3,83)&41&(3,163)\\
2&(3,7)&22&(7,83)&42&(3,167)\\
3&(3,11)&23&(5,89)&43&(7,167)\\
4&(5,13)&24&(19,79)&44&(5,173)\\
5&(3,19)&25&(5,97)&45&(3,179)\\
6&(3,23)&26&(3,103)&46&(5,181)\\
7&(7,23)&27&(3,107)&47&(11,179)\\
8&(3,31)&28&(5,109)&48&(3,191)\\
9&(7,31)&29&(5,113)&49&(5,193)\\
10&(5,37)&30&(13,109)&50&(3,199)\\
11&(3,43)&31&(13,113)&51&(7,199)\\
12&(3,47)&32&(3,127)&52&(11,199)\\
13&(7,47)&33&(3,131)&53&(3,211)\\
14&(5,53)&34&(7,131)&54&(7,211)\\
15&(3,59)&35&(3,139)&55&(11,211)\\
16&(5,61)&36&(7,139)&56&(3,223)\\
17&(3,67)&37&(11,139)&57&(3,227)\\
18&(3,71)&38&(3,151)&58&(5,229)\\
19&(5,73)&39&(7,151)&59&(5,233)\\
20&(3,79)&40&(5,157)&&
\end{array}
\]
For every row, direct addition gives \(p+q=4k+2\). Every displayed summand is prime; this is a finite primality check, for example by checking that none has a prime divisor at most its square root. Thus the desired conclusion holds throughout \(1\le k<60\).

It remains to consider \(k\ge60\). Set
\[
n=2k+1.
\]
This number is odd, and
\[
n=2k+1\ge121>120.
\]
Consequently, hypothesis (2) gives \(A(n)\ne0\). Also \(n>0\), so the lemma supplies primes \(p,q\) satisfying
\[
p+q=2n.
\]
Substituting \(n=2k+1\), we obtain
\[
p+q=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]
Hence \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes for every \(k\ge60\) as well.

Combining this with the explicit finite range proves that, under the conjecture that \(A(n)\ne0\) for every odd \(n>120\), every integer of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is the sum of two primes.
